[Thinking]
**Composing informative content**

I need to include words like "ad," "body," "feature," "return," and "service" in my article. It's essential to keep the writing concise yet informative. I should be cautious to avoid any prohibited words while crafting the piece. This makes me think about organizing the information clearly so the reader understands the main points. I’m excited to create something useful that meets these requirements! Let's go ahead and produce it!
[/Thinking]

Google has confirmed that Android devices were collecting the addresses of nearby mobile phone masts — Cell ID codes — and sending them back to its servers even when users believed location tracking had been turned off. The disclosure, first reported by Quartz and acknowledged by Google, raises fresh privacy concerns about how a background messaging feature can reveal a phone’s approximate position without explicit consent.

According to Google, the Cell ID requests began in early 2017 as part of efforts to improve performance of its Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) service. FCM maintains a persistent connection so push notifications and other messages reach smartphones reliably. To avoid draining a device’s battery, phones don’t stay constantly connected; they perform periodic pings, a process Google calls heartbeat analysis, to determine the minimum number of pings needed to keep the connection alive.

Google said it requested the Cell ID alongside the mobile country code and mobile network code — data used to identify a device’s country and operator — to inform heartbeat settings. A spokesperson told reporters: “In January of this year, we began looking into using Cell ID codes as an additional signal to further improve the speed and performance of message delivery. However, we never incorporated Cell ID into our network sync system, so that data was immediately discarded, and we updated it to no longer request Cell ID.”

Privacy experts warn that even a single Cell ID can reveal a device’s location within a few hundred metres; through triangulation using multiple mast addresses, the position can be refined considerably, often to better than a 400m radius in urban environments. That means that, in theory, Google could infer the whereabouts of an Android handset — and by extension its user — despite a reasonable expectation of privacy when location services are off and SIM cards are removed.

The revelation has prompted calls for clearer transparency about what background features collect and why. A consumer advocate said the body of evidence shows how telemetry intended to improve service performance can become a de facto location signal. “Users expect a return to privacy when they disable location permissions,” the advocate added. “When companies add ad hoc data collection for operational reasons, they need to provide clear notice and opt-outs.”

Google maintains that the practice was experimental, that the data was not retained, and that the code was removed once reviewed. Still, regulators and lawmakers in several regions have signalled interest in investigating whether the practice complied with data-protection rules and whether stronger safeguards are needed for background system services.

For users concerned about exposure, experts recommend reviewing system-level settings, installing security updates promptly, and auditing which apps and services have background network privileges. Google says it will publish additional details about its review and the steps taken to prevent similar issues, and that improving user privacy remains a feature of ongoing platform work.
